text: Atlantic slave trade

source.page_title: The sea in culture

text: In the Atlantic slave trade , enslaved people , mostly from central and western Africa and usually sold by West Africans to European slave traders , were carried across the sea , mainly to the Americas .

source.page_title: The sea in culture

text: The slave trade regularly used the triangular trade route from Europe ( with manufactured goods ) to West Africa and on to the Americas ( with slaves ) , and then back to Europe ( with goods such as sugar ) .

source.page_title: The sea in culture

text: The South Atlantic and Caribbean economies depended on a secure supply of labour for agriculture and manufacturing of goods to sell in Europe , and in turn the European economy depended in large part on the profits from the trade .

source.page_title: The sea in culture

text: Some 12 million Africans arrived in the Americas , and many more died on the journey , powerfully influencing the culture of the Americas .

source.page_title: The sea in culture

text: Burial at sea

source.page_title: The sea in culture

text: The burial of entire or cremated bodies at sea has been practised by countries around the world since ancient times , with instances recorded from the ancient civilisations in Egypt , Greece , and Rome .

source.page_title: The sea in culture

text: Practices vary by country and by religion ; for example , the United States allows human remains to be buried at sea at least three nautical miles from land , and if the remains are uncremated the water must be at least 600 feet deep , while in Islam burial by lowering a weighted clay vessel into the sea is permitted when a person dies on a ship .

text: The seamstress is a fictional character in Charles Dickens 's 1859 novel A Tale of Two Cities .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: The seamstress is an unnamed twenty - year - old woman featured as a desperately poor peasant accused of plotting against the French Republic by Robespierre 's Committee of Public Safety during the Terror of the French Revolution in 1793 .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: Found guilty of this imaginary crime , she was condemned to death by beheading .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: She became acquainted with Charles Darnay during their imprisonments in La Force Prison , and was the only person to recognize Sydney Carton as an impostor as the two of them rode to their execution together .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: She spends her last moments conversing with Carton noting that he provides strength to her .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: The Republic executes her as the 22nd of fifty - two to be killed that day .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: Sydney Carton dies directly after her .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: Character analysis

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: The seamstress is described as " a young woman , with a slight girlish form , a sweet spare face in which there was no vestige of color , and large widely opened patient eyes " .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: She often denotes herself as " poor , " " little , " " ignorant , " and " weak " .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: Although she says she is weak , she maintains a calm temperament through her last moments as Dickens often describes her hands , eyes , and face as " patient " .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: Her calm disposition only breaks once as she tells Carton of her cousin , five years her junior , who is her only familial relative .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: She remains calm as she describes that they have been separated by poverty and that her cousin will not know of her fate , but begins to tear up as she wonders if it will be a long wait before she sees her again in heaven .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: She is understanding and accepting of the Republic even as she is sentenced to death .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: She states , " I am not unwilling to die , if the Republic which is to do so much good to us poor , will profit by my death " .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: She only references the Republic once more as she mentions her cousin in that the Republic may extend her cousin 's life to old age .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: Relationship with Sydney Carton

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: After she realizes that Carton has sacrificed himself for Darnay , she calls him " brave and generous " .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: They share a brief kiss before she goes to die .

source.page_title: The seamstress (A Tale of Two Cities)

text: Literary significance and criticism Doris Y. Kadish describes the seamstress as " a humble heroine of the revolution , " while " Lisa Robson ( Modern Criticism , pp. 97 -101 ) and other feminist critics draw on late - twentieth century studies of the role of women in the French Revolution to offer new perspectives on ... the seamstress ... " and Beth Harris writes that " the anonymous seamstress in A Tale of Two Cities , who has ' done nothing , ' re-establishes a narrative horizon that charts its length along the great actions of men ... "

text: In 1623 , Anne and Little James were the third and fourth ships financed by the London - based Company of Merchant Adventurers to travel together to North America in support of the Plymouth Colony , following Mayflower in 1620 and Fortune in 1621 .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Anne carried mostly passengers , while the much smaller Little James carried primarily cargo , albeit with a few passengers as well .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: After a stormy three - month voyage from England , Anne arrived at New Plymouth in early July 1623 , with Little James arriving a week or so later .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Between them the ships brought 90 - odd new settlers , along with about thirty others who were not part of the core emigrant group .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Many of this emigrant contingent would serve the colony well in the coming years , while others would be judged unfit for the hardships of colony life and be sent back to England .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Anne Anne was a supply ship of about 140 tons displacement which was used in 1623 , along with Little James , to deliver a large party of new settlers to the newly founded Plymouth Colony .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Anne was the larger of the two ships and most of the passengers traveled in her .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Anne 's master was William Peirce , a young man of Ratcliffe , London who was a member of the Adventurers investment group and had made many trans - Atlantic voyages .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: William Bradford , quoted by author Charles Edward Banks , gives the date of arrival of Anne at Plymouth as being July 10 , 1623 , with the pinnace Little James 's arrival being , per Bradford , “ ..about a week or so after came in the pinnass ( sic ) . ”

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Author Caleb Johnson reports that Little James arrived in Plymouth on August 5 , 1623 .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Soon after arrival , the crew of Anne went to work loading whatever timber and beaver skins could be provided as cargo and sailed straight back across the Atlantic to home .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Little James Little James was a full - rigged pinnace of forty - four tons displacement , and for her voyage to America she had come brand - new from the builder ’s yard .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Per Bradford : “ a fine new vessel of about 44 .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: tunne , which the Company had built to stay in the Countrie . ”

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: She was a small ship with about one - quarter the tonnage of Anne and a total crew of probably not more than fifteen men .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Her nominal captain was Emmanuel Altham , a 23 - year - old Englishman of the landed gentry from Essexshire , a Merchant Adventurer , and a novice at the business of sailing .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The actual sailing of Little James was put in the charge of a master mariner , John Bridges .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Little James 's primary purpose on the voyage to New Plymouth was to carry company cargo but she did have about fifteen known passengers .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: In later years Bradford wrote about the little ship that “ I fear the adventurers did over - pride themselves in her .. for she had ill success . ”

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: When the crew of Little James signed on for the voyage , they agreed to spend six years in Plymouth Colony , but as shareholders instead of wage earners .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: What they expected was to make money by receiving a share of the ship ’s profits from fishing and trading , with the ship ’s investors paying for the crew ’s food , drink and clothing .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The armament of Little James consisted of six small cannons with a bore of two inches which could fire a ball of a few pounds in weight .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Her men had six muskets between them .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: And because the ship was armed , the crew believed they had a chance to take prize ships of enemy nations such as France or Spain as far south as the West Indies .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: But the crew was disappointed to find that under the law of the sea , prizes could only be taken if the ship had letters of marque issued by the Crown , and Little James had none .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: En route from England to Plymouth , Captain Altham refused to capture a French ship sailing home to New Rochelle in France , which caused his crew much vexation .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: On board Little James were two crewmen who would go on to cause a great deal of trouble and end up in an Admiralty inquiry : a gunner named William Stephens ( or Stevens ) and a carpenter named Thomas Fell , both of whom knew how badly the ship needed their services .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: After arriving at New Plymouth and seeing the shabby state of the colony and condition of the colonists , some working and others merely idling , the crew believed they had been fooled .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: At that , Stephens and Fell led the crew to go on strike to demand an interim payment of cash .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: William Bradford managed to calm them down , but only after he offered to personally pay them himself .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Working on the coast of New England , Little James had two major problems .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: First , the investment company ( Merchant Adventurers ) had neglected to provide the ship with any trade goods , making it close to impossible to obtain any prime furs to ship to England .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Second , the ship was “ rudely manned ” by a crew that was not happy with their financial situation of being paid in company shares in lieu of true wages .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The Merchant Adventurers who had sent Little James had hoped to have their expenses reimbursed with a trade in furs above all else , as furs were the only item of New World export expected to return a profit .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: As things turned out , the search for skins was totally futile .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: By late 1623 things were not going well for the purposes for which Little James was brought to the colony .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: She sailed around Cape Cod seeking Indian trade relations , and as far as modern Rhode Island , but Altham lacked the quality trade goods that the natives wanted in exchange for furs .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Nor could he compete with the very active Dutch traders , who could offer the natives a better price .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: As Little James returned from Rhode Island , the weather was calm , so her master anchored the ship at the entrance to Plymouth harbor .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: A gale quickly arose and the ship lost the grip of her anchors .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The ship was headed toward a dangerous sand bank known as Brown ’s Bank when the crew chopped through the mainmast and cut away the rigging , thereby saving it .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: With her mast and tackle gone , the ship anchored again ( Johnson reports that anchors were lost ) , with the anchors holding until the wind changed and she could enter the harbor .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The company was forced to provide Little James with a new mast , and refit her with anchors and rigging .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Plymouth Harbor is where the ship spent the rest of the winter of 1623 – 1624 , in freezing weather with the crew existing on short rations , apart from some wildfowl and with only cold water to drink , when alcohol was the drink of choice at the time .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: During that long bitter winter discipline on Little James collapsed completely .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The wreck of Little James

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: In the spring of 1624 , Altham took Little James east to Maine with a sullen , hungry , and mutinous crew .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: While anchored at Pemaquid on a fishing and trading expedition , the crew mutinied and threatened Altham and master Bridges with the destruction of the ship .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The crew forced Altham to go back to New Plymouth by small boat to find food .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: With the help of senior Pilgrim Edward Winslow , Altham rushed back to Pemaquid with some bread and peas .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: They were within a day ’s sail of reaching Little James when they found that a second storm had disabled the ship in the harbor at Damariscove Island ( now in Maine ) where English seamen maintained a small fishing station .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: On the night of April 10 , 1624 , during another storm , the ship lost the grip of her anchors on the sea floor once again when wind and waves caused her to crash onto rocks and topple over .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: As the ship went over , two large holes were opened in her structure , drowning master John Bridges in the wreck and killing two crewmen , John Vow and Peter Morrett , when their escape boat capsized and was struck by Little James 's falling mainyard .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Again Stephens and Fell mutinied and refused to help save the ship .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Fortunately the masters of several other ships in port at Damariscove were available to inspect the Little James wreck and found she was fit for salvage .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: They contacted William Bradford offering to salvage the ship if the Colony would meet their bill in beaver skins .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Bradford sent the furs and work began with ship ’s carpenters and coopers making great water - tight barrels which were tied to Little James and with that help the ship , with rising waters , was lifted off the rocks .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: All hands worked to haul the ship to a secure location where craftsmen made repairs at great expense to the Company .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Within six weeks of the shipwreck , Little James was ready for sea again .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: But by this time the investors had become thoroughly frustrated by the misadventures of Little James which had become quite costly to repair instead of making a good profit as was intended .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: At this point William Bradford decided to send the ship and its crew back to England .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The wreck had been a tragedy not only for the ship but also for her captain .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: In the wreck , the ship had lost her four small boats , very important for doing coastal trading business , as well as her salt , codfish , and all her supplies and trading goods .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Captain Altham lost all his precious books and most of his belongings .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: When the ship did reach London , Fell and Stephens left it “ in the river of Thames in very disordered and evil manner . ”

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: They also promptly sued the investor group and Plymouth Colony for forty pounds , in the form of wages that William Bradford had promised and apparently not paid .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The monies they demanded amounted to 4 – 6 years of wages they should have received , notwithstanding the fact that they had mutinied and refused to help the ship and other crew when they were most needed .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: High Court of Admiralty , November 1624 Lawsuits over Little James began as soon as the ship arrived back in England .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The High Court of Admiralty , which had jurisdiction over maritime matters , took custody of the ship and all her goods and furnishings pending the outcome of these lawsuits .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Two of the larger investors in the Pilgrim ’s joint - stock company , Thomas Fletcher and Thomas Goffe , had invested most of the money involved in building and outfitting Little James , and now wanted possession of the ship as payment for that debt , in addition to crewmen Stephens and Fell wanting their back wages .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Noted Mayflower author Caleb Johnson , writing in the March 2011 issue of The Mayflower Quarterly , provided information from extensive research of English records over the Little James affair .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Johnson states that a number of depositions and other Admiralty records have survived in the case of Stephens and Fell vs. Little James .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The following is an extract of some of Johnson ’s article , including depositions by Edward Winslow .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Surviving depositions were made to the Court by : 1 . Edward Winslow , Mayflower passenger and occasional Plymouth Colony governor .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: 2 . William Peirce , master of Anne that came to Plymouth in 1623 .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: 3 . Benedict Morgan , one of the passengers on Fortune that came to Plymouth in 1621 .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: 4 . Robert Cushman , one of the leading members of the Leiden delegation .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: 5 . James Sherley , one of many investors in the company and later treasurer .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Johnson reprinted in his March 2011 The Mayflower Quarterly article two depositions by Edward Winslow – although the charges to which Winslow had nothing to depose are not stated here – only those of which Winslow had knowledge :

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: First deposition by Edward Winslow dated 17 November 1624 , which states that he was Edward Winslow of Plymouth in New England , yeoman , aged thirty years or thereabouts .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: He confirmed that when the Little James arrived in New England , Edmund ( sic ) Altham was captain and John Bridges master of her and upon arrival in Plymouth the captain and master of the Little James complained about troublesome crewmen Stevens ( Stephens ) and Fell .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: This also concerned Stephens and Fells wage complaint , with Winslow deposing knowledge of their dispute over wages .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Also that he heard that the two men did not help during the wreck at Pemmaquid which included loss of the ship ’s equipment and stores worth about four or five hundred pounds .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: He also was deposed about the loss of four shallops ( small boats ) and another boat lost at another time and negligence of her crew .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: He also noted an instance of rowdy behavior by Stevens in Plymouth .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: In the second deposition by Edward Winslow ( undated ) he stated that he was an Adventurer investing the amount of “ three score pounds in the plantation ” .. “ and hath been an Adventurer therein since the beginning of it . “

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: He also confirmed that when the Little James arrived at New England , Stevens was gunner and Fell was the carpenter .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Additionally , he confirmed there was a dispute by Stevens and Fell over wages but the sum of the wages he knew not .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: He also confirmed that when the ship sunk all the ship ’s victuals ( food stores ) perished , but of the crew that did not forsake the ship and “ all that would stick to her in distress ” were relieved when necessary victuals were provided by neighbor fishermen with payment to be made by the Company which was cleared by the Captain and this respondent ( Winslow ) .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Lastly , he deposed that he heard that when the ship was sunk “ some of the neighbors thereabouts ” did wish all ship crew members “ disperse themselves into the Country and work for their passage ” and some did disperse themselves “ and others stayed by her and labored in the recovery of her . ”

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: By the trading season of 1625 Little James was again sailing the Atlantic in support of Plymouth Colony , investors having sent her and another ship over to fish for cod .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: At that time , the Colony had debts in the amount of thirteen hundred pounds , and to settle these debts , they needed to ship three thousand beaver pelts to England , this quantity being too far beyond their ability to collect .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: But the Colony did arrange for Little James to transport about five hundred beaver furs back to England to assist in paying their debts .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: But in the continuing ill - fortune for Little James , the cargo never reached its intended English port .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Somewhere in the English Channel , almost within sight of the English coast , Little James was captured by pirates with all her cargo taken and with the valuable beaver pelts being sold cheaply for four pence each in the North African Barbary pirate bazaars of Algiers or Tunis .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Little James , which was built by the Adventurers to remain in New England , could have been of great assistance to the colonists in matters of trade and fishing , but seemed to have endless ill fortune ( see the following for the fate of her captain ) which included lack of support by the investors , a mutinous crew , a shipwreck , seizure by the Admiralty Court and creditors in England and finally capture by Barbary pirates .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The loss of the ship was something that hurt the Pilgrims greatly , as their harvest had prospered but their trade had not , due to a lack of ships to carry on trade with England , and could only send fur pelts home in small quantities .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: The passengers

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Per Bradford 's later recollection , 60 persons — men , women and children — were on the two ships Anne and Little James combined , although in reality the number of passengers was much more than that .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: There are no separate passenger lists for Anne and for Little James as those who came over on these ships were grouped together in official records when the 1623 division of land was made for them .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: But author Charles Banks did identify at least four men , three with families , who were passengers in Little James .

source.page_title: The ships Anne and Little James

text: Banks goes on to state that it is possible that Little James had more passengers , but due to her size could not accommodate many .

text: The simExchange is a web - based prediction market in which players use virtual money to buy and sell stocks and futures contracts in upcoming video game properties .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The main purpose of the web site is to predict trends in the video game industry , particularly how upcoming products will sell and how they will be received by the critics .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: For those who do not participate in the prediction market , the web site is a database of sales forecasts and game quality forecasts that are updated in real - time .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The web site also features a number of " Wisdom of the crowd " - type content collaboration and aggregation tools , including means for sharing information , articles , images , and videos about the games .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: How it works

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The prediction market works as a stock market game for players to predict the number of units a game or console hardware will sell or the reviews a game will receive .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: These predictions are made by trading global lifetime sales stocks , NPD Futures , and Metacritic Futures .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: These tradable contracts directly forecast the metric , for example :

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: If a stock is priced at 100 DKP , this corresponds to a forecast of 1 million units .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: If a trader believes the product will sell more than 1 million units , then he would buy the stock , if he believes the product will sell less than 1 million units , then he would sell the stock .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: In this way , the simExchange is a type of stock market game .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The website also features a number of user tools to aggregate and display information about video games and publishers .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: In addition to a message board for each game , the simExchange advertises the ability of users to submit relevant news articles , and to append images and videos of a game to its page .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Users may also vote on the importance of such submitted content by spending 100DKP to place either an " up bid " or a " down bid " on the content , receiving a 100DKP payout every time another user votes in the same way .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Down bids were removed from the system in August 2009 as a result of user feedback .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: In this way , the simExchange is also a social news website .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: In March 2010 , a number of these content submission tools , such as the ability to submit images and video , were removed due to lack of use , although the features remain advertised in the site 's tutorials .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: DKP DKP is the name of the virtual currency used on the simExchange .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The currency was named after the dragon kill points used in many massively multiplayer online games .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Unlike some forms of virtual currency , DKP is not backed by real money .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Types of contracts

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The simExchange aims to predict both the quantitative and qualitative sides of the video game industry .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: It originally launched with only stocks that forecast the global lifetime sales of gaming products .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: On April 12 , 2007 , the simExchange began public testing of monthly sales futures contracts , which later became known as NPD Futures .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Metacritic Futures were similarly introduced in September of the same year .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: As of September 2010 , the simExchange has deactivated both futures contracts , again only offers trading in stocks .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: A stock on the simExchange , also referred to as a Global Lifetime Sales stock or simply a GLS stock , represents the total global unit sales a video game product will sell through to consumers over the product 's lifetime .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: These stocks do not have a pre-determined expiration date as some games can sell for years .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: For global lifetime stocks , 1DKP equals 10,000 copies of that game sold .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: For example , if a trader thinks a game will sell 234,000 copies , that would correlate to a stock price of 23.40 DKP .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: NPD Futures

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: An NPD Futures Contract was a virtual contract that predicted the sales data the NPD Group released on a monthly basis .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: These futures covered the NPD Group 's data on console hardware sales , game sales , and total software sales .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: These contracts would cease trading one day before NPD reports were made public , and pay out at the end of the following day .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The price of NPD Futures Contracts was similar to those of stocks , with 1DKP price corresponding to 10,000 units sold .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: For example , if the Xbox 360 November Futures Contract is priced at 60.00 DKP , this corresponds to a forecast of 600,000 units will be sold in the retail month of November .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The simExchange stopped offering NPD Futures Contracts after September 2010 , although the archives of all forecasts up until this point are still available on the simExchange website .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The discontinuation of this service corresponded with the NPD Group 's decision to cease publicly releasing hardware and software unit sales numbers .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Metacritic Futures A Metacritic Futures Contract is a virtual contract that predicts the score a game will receive from review aggregation website Metacritic .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Despite not being directly based on sales data , Metacritic scores have been shown to be highly indicative of a game 's sales .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: These contracts cease trading and pay out 14 days after the game 's release .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: A Metacritic Future 's price is directly related to the Metacritic score .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: For example , a 90.00 DKP price would correspond to a forecast of a 90 score on Metacritic .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The simExchange stopped offering Metacritic Futures after July 2009 due to lack of user interest in trading the contracts .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Applications Data produced by the simExchange has been noted as a resource for real - world investors .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The metrics that are forecast are fundamental factors that drive the stocks of the companies that produce the games .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: The simExchange 's prediction market data has been used by Wall Street analysts , such as Michael Pachter , in their published notes and financial news outlets , such as Reuters , MarketWatch , and TheStreet.com .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Given the current status of the website , it is unlikely that the simExchange 's data is still influential or relevant .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Current status Users of the simExchange noticed a " sharp decline " in the number of users in 2010 , after NPD Futures were no longer offered as part of the game , and site upkeep slowed to a crawl by mid-2011 .

source.page_title: The simExchange

text: Although the game still has players , users have described it as everything from " dead " to " a ghost town . "

text: In Buddhist literature , the sixteen frightening dreams of King Pasenadi ( Sanskrit ; Pali Mahāsupina Jātaka ) is notable topic of Buddhism and dreamt by the King Pasenadi of Kosala and their Interpretations by the Gautama Buddha .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Buddha used Anāgatam Nyandaw ( အနာဂတံ ဉာဏ်တော် ) to visualise the nightmares .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Then he explained that the nightmares are the terrible things that will happen in the future .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: When the time reaches after 2500 Sāsanā Years ( သာသနာနှစ် ) or circa 1957 A.D , the foretold events will take place .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The pictures depicting the sixteen nightmares are found in some pagodas in Myanmar .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The 16 frightening dreams

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: First dream

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The four strong oxen , from North , East , South and West , came to fight against one another in front of the king .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: But when they are about to fight , they retreated instead .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : " When bad people lead , the dark clouds came to rain , but just thunder instead , thus destroying certain crops and leading people to starve . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Second dream

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The young plants are bearing fruits .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : " When people begin to have short lifespan , young people will marry and have kids even when they are below 18 years old . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Mahārāja , imassā pi vipāko lokassa parihāyanakāle manussānaṁ parittāyukakāle bhavissati .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Anāgatasmiñhi sattā tibbarāgā bhavissanti , asampattavayāva kumāriyo purisantaraṁ gantvā utuniyo ceva gabbhiniyo ca hutvā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhissanti .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Khuddakarukkhānaṁ pupphaṁ viya hi tāsaṁ utunibhāvo , phalaṁ viya ca puttadhītaro bhavissanti .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: " Great King , as a result of this , when the world is declining , the lifespan of humans will decrease .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , beings will have strong desires , and young girls , not having found partners , will go to men out of season , and they will grow up with sons and daughters .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Like the flowers of small trees , their youthfulness will be short - lived , and like fruits , their sons and daughters will be few . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Third dream

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The female cow feeds on the milk of her child .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : " When people stop respecting the elders , the parents will live with their children , for not having anyone to rely on . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Imassā pi vipāko anāgate eva manussānaṁ jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammassa naṭṭhakāle bhavissati .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Anāgatasmiñhi sattā mātāpitūsu vā sassusasuresu vā lajjaṁ anupaṭṭhāpetvā sayam - eva kuṭumbaṁ saṁvidahantāva ghāsacchādanamattam - pi mahallakānaṁ dātukāmā dassanti , adātukāmā na dassanti .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Mahallakā anāthā asayaṁvasī dārake ārādhetvā jīvissanti tadahujātānaṁ vacchakānaṁ khīraṁ pivantiyo mahāgāviyo viya .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Itonidānam - pi te bhayaṁ natthi , catutthaṁ kathehi , mahārājāti .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: This consequence will also occur in the future when respect for elders is lost among humans .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , beings will neither feel shame towards their parents nor their parents - in - law .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will only take care of their own households and will give even the bare necessities of food and clothing to the elderly only if they wish to , and will not give if they do not wish to .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The elderly will live dependent on the goodwill of children , just as large cows live on the milk from calves born that very day .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Because of this , they will have no protection .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Fourth dream A farmer is using young cows for transportation and abandons strong ones .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : " People will hire young , inexperienced people in certain jobs , especially judging crimes .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Not being able to work well , the young people will quit the jobs and old people will not reapply for their previous jobs , which leads to the demise of a country . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Imassā pi vipāko anāgate eva adhammikarājūnaṁ kāle bhavissati .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Anāgatasmiñhi adhammikakapaṇarājāno paṇḍitānaṁ paveṇikusalānaṁ kammaṁ nittharaṇasamatthānaṁ mahāmattānaṁ yasaṁ na dassanti .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Dhammasabhāyaṁ vinicchayaṭṭhāne pi paṇḍite vohārakusale mahallake amacce na ṭhapessanti , tabbiparītānaṁ pana taruṇataruṇānaṁ yasaṁ dassanti , tathārūpe eva vinicchayaṭṭhāne ṭhapessanti , te rājakammāni ceva yuttāyuttañca ajānantā neva taṁ yasaṁ ukkhipituṁ sakkhissanti , na rājakammāni nittharituṁ .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Te asakkontā kammadhuraṁ chaḍḍessanti , mahallakā pi paṇḍitāmaccā yasaṁ alabhantā kiccāni nittharituṁ samatthāpi : “ Kiṁ amhākaṁ etehi , mayaṁ bāhirakā jātā , abbhantarikā taruṇadārakā jānissantī ” ti { 1.338} uppannāni kammāni na karissanti , evaṁ sabbathā pi tesaṁ rājūnaṁ hāni yeva bhavissati , dhuraṁ vahituṁ asamatthānaṁ vacchadammānaṁ dhure yojitakālo viya , dhuravāhānañca mahāgoṇānaṁ yugaparamparāya ayojitakālo viya bhavissati .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: This consequence will also occur in the future during the time of unjust kings .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , unjust and poor kings will not honor the deserving officials , those skilled in ancestral knowledge , and those capable of completing tasks .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the court of law , they will not appoint wise and skilled elders as ministers , but will instead bestow honor upon the opposite type , appointing young and inexperienced individuals in their places .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: These inexperienced officials , ignorant of what is right and wrong , will neither be able to sustain their positions nor complete the king 's tasks .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Failing to manage their responsibilities , they will abandon their duties .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The wise and capable elder ministers , though able to complete the tasks , will think , '' What use are these tasks to us ?

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: We are outsiders ; the young insiders will know what to do , ' and will not undertake the tasks that arise .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Thus , the kings will invariably face decline , much like when calves are yoked to carry a heavy load or when a series of oxen fit for heavy labor are not yoked together . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The horse with two heads eats wheat from two different containers instead of eating together .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : Evil judges will take the bribery of both the defendant and the jurors , and they will decide the crimes however they want . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Imassā pi anāgate adhammikarājakāle yeva vipāko bhavissati .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Anāgatasmiñhi adhammikā bālarājāno adhammike lolamanusse vinicchaye ṭhapessanti , te pāpapuññesu anādarā bālā sabhāyaṁ nisīditvā vinicchayaṁ dentā ubhinnam - pi atthapaccatthikānaṁ hatthato lañjaṁ gahetvā khādissanti asso viya dvīhi mukhehi yavasaṁ .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , unjust and foolish kings will appoint greedy and unprincipled people to positions of judgment .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: These foolish individuals , disregarding good and bad deeds , will sit in court and make decisions while taking bribes from both parties involved in disputes , eating like a horse with two mouths . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Sixth dream People encourage a wolf to urinate on the golden cup .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : " Good people will not be respected or praised , thus reducing reputation .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: So , they have to make friends with bad people for the sake of their reputation . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: 6 ) Imassā pi vipāko anāgate yeva bhavissati .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Anāgatasmiñhi adhammikā papi rājāno dhammika kulaputtānaṁ āsaṅkāya yasaṁ na dassanti , adhammika kulaputtānaṁ yeva dassanti .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: 6 ) " This consequence will also occur in the future .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , unjust and wicked kings will not honor righteous noble sons due to distrust but will instead favor unrighteous noble sons .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Thus , great families will fall into poverty , while inferior families will become powerful .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Those noblemen , unable to sustain themselves , will say , ' We will live by depending on these people , ' and will give their daughters in marriage to wicked men .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Therefore , the association of noble daughters with wicked men will be like placing a golden bowl in front of an old jackal . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: A hungry , female wolf tries to eat the thread without letting him know .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : " Women will not consider about the money their husbands have tiredly made .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will spend the money for clothes , food , drinks , jewelry and gambling without letting their husbands know . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Imassā pi anāgate yeva vipāko bhavissati .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Anāgatasmiñhi itthiyo purisalolā surālolā alaṅkāralolā visikhālolā āmisalolā bhavissanti dussīlā durācārā , tā sāmikehi kasigorakkhādīni kammāni katvā kicchena kasirena sambhataṁ dhanaṁ jārehi saddhiṁ suraṁ pivantiyo mālāgandhavilepanaṁ dhārayamānā antogehe accāyikam - pi kiccaṁ anoloketvā gehe parikkhepassa uparibhāgena pi chiddaṭṭhānehi pi jāre upadhārayamānā sve vapitabbayuttakaṁ bījam - pi koṭṭetvā yāgubhattakhajjakādīni sampādetvā khādamānā vilumpissanti heṭṭhāpīṭhake nipannachātasiṅgālī viya vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā pādamūle nikkhittarajjuṁ .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , women will be attached to men , alcohol , ornaments , streets , and material things .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will be immoral and of bad conduct .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will entertain lovers in their homes , through holes and cracks in the walls .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will use the seeds meant for the next day 's planting to prepare porridge , rice , and snacks , thus depleting the household resources .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will squander the household wealth , rolling around like hungry jackals lying down on the ground , with the rope lying at their feet . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: There is a large pot surrounded with other small pots .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Meaning : " People will experience poverty because of their evil leaders .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They have to work hard for their leaders and not for their family which leads to starvation . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The outcome of this dream will come in the future .

text: In the future , there will be unjust kings , and among them , both the just and unjust , the rulers , Brahmins , householders , and people will all become unjust .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Then , even the protective deities , those who accept offerings , tree deities , and deities in space will also become unjust .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The winds under the rule of unjust kings will be erratic and harsh , causing the celestial palaces to shake .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: When these palaces shake , the deities , angered by the shaking , will refuse to let rain fall .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Even if it rains throughout the entire kingdom , it will rain only in one place , or it will not rain at all .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Even if there is rainfall , it will not be beneficial for agriculture or cultivation .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Just as in a kingdom , so too in the countryside , villages , towns , and cities , there will be no uniform rainfall .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the upper regions , there will be excessive rainfall , while in the lower regions , there will be none .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In one part , crops will perish due to excessive rain , while in another , they will wither due to lack of rain .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: One area will suffer from drought , while another will be flooded .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: One king 's reign will resemble a pot filled with rice that is neither fully cooked nor uncooked . "

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , there will be many shameless monks who are greedy for the support of others .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will teach the Dhamma for the sake of robes and other requisites , using flattery and pleasing speech to entice others .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will not be capable of teaching for the sake of liberation , having become intoxicated by their support .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: They will only say , " Having heard sweet words and received valuable robes , they will show favor . "

text: Others will sit at the doors of royal chambers and other places , teaching for the sake of coins and wealth .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Thus , having made the Dhamma a commodity , and for the sake of coins and wealth , they will sell it , like those who sell sandalwood essence for a hundred thousand coins , with the intention of filling their bellies .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: In the future , there will indeed be consequences as society declines .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: Both within households and in the broader society , there will be widespread violence and exploitation , all for the pursuit of material wealth .

source.page_title: The sixteen dreams of King Pasenadi

text: The phrase " the son of man came to serve " refers to a specific episode in the New Testament .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: In the Gospel of Matthew 20:20 – 28 and the Gospel of Mark 10:35 – 45 , Jesus explains that he " came as Son of man to give his life as ransom " .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: The ransom paid by the Son of man is an element of a common doctrine of atonement in Christianity .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: In the Gospel of Mark 10:35 – 45 , this episode takes place shortly after Jesus predicts his death , and then says :

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them , and their high officials exercise authority over them .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: Not so with you .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: Instead , whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant , and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: For even the Son of Man did not come to be served , but to serve , and to give his life as a ransom for many .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: In the Gospel of Luke 22:24 – 27 , Jesus expounds on the import of serving :

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: A dispute also arose among them as to which of them was considered to be greatest .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: Jesus said to them , " The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them ; and those who exercise authority over them call themselves Benefactors .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: But you are not to be like that .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: Instead , the greatest among you should be like the youngest , and the one who rules like the one who serves .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: For who is greater , the one who is at the table or the one who serves ?

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: Is it not the one who is at the table ?

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: But I am among you as one who serves . "

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: The identification of Jesus with the son of man in the context of the Book of Daniel ( 7:13 – 14 ) places the death of Jesus and the ransom he pays at a higher level of prominence than the death of other prophets and martyrs , even that of his contemporary John the Baptist .

source.page_title: The son of man came to serve

text: Later in the New Testament account , in Matthew 26:63 – 64 , when Jesus considers himself the son of man spoken of in the Book of Daniel , the Jewish high priests accuse him of blasphemy .

text: The spider and the fly problem is a recreational mathematics problem with an unintuitive solution , asking for a shortest path or geodesic between two points on the surface of a cuboid .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: It was originally posed by Henry Dudeney .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: In the typical version of the puzzle , an otherwise empty cuboid room 30 feet long , 12 feet wide and 12 feet high contains a spider and a fly .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: The spider is 1 foot below the ceiling and horizontally centred on one 12 ′ × 12 ′ wall .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: The fly is 1 foot above the floor and horizontally centred on the opposite wall .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: The problem is to find the minimum distance the spider must crawl along the walls , ceiling and / or floor to reach the fly , which remains stationary .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: A naive solution is for the spider to remain horizontally centred , and crawl up to the ceiling , across it and down to the fly , giving a distance of 42 feet .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: Instead , the shortest path , 40 feet long , spirals around five of the six faces of the cuboid .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: Alternatively , it can be described by unfolding the cuboid into a net and finding a shortest path ( a line segment ) on the resulting unfolded system of six rectangles in the plane .

source.page_title: The spider and the fly problem

text: Different nets produce different segments with different lengths , and the question becomes one of finding a net whose segment length is minimum .

text: " The talk " is a colloquial expression for a conversation black parents in the United States feel compelled to have with their children and teenagers about the dangers they face due to racism or unjust treatment from authority figures , law enforcement or other parties , and how to de-escalate them .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: The practice dates back generations and is often viewed as a rite of passage for black children .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: History Black youth in the United States have historically been instructed by their parents or other caregivers on the dangers they face due to racism .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Variations of the talk have been conducted in black families for decades or generations ; the practice " dates back to slavery and has lasted centuries " .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: The talk has evolved .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: In the 1940s , the talk might have covered avoiding certain neighborhoods .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: In the 1980s , it might have covered " how to dress , walk and act and to be mindful of how others could perceive them " .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: In the 2010s it typically focused on interactions with the police .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Utne Reader called the talk " a rite of passage " for black children .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Judy Belk , writing in the Los Angeles Times , called the talk " an unfair but necessary burden we carry in the black community , one we reluctantly pass down " and " a painful ritual . "

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: In 2020 , during and after the George Floyd protests , some black commentators called for white parents to have a similar talk with their children on how to behave when they witness racist behavior and how to be anti-racist .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Later that year , during the final 2020 United States presidential debate , moderator Kristen Welker asked both candidates to express their opinions on the talk .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: The conversation often focuses on how to de-escalate encounters with police especially given the high frequency of black men being pulled over for minor , insignificant or non-existent issues , also referred to as driving while black .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Sometimes the talk addresses encounters with white supremacists or vigilantes .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: The " talk " has been described as an example of preparation for bias in racial - ethnic socialization and typically addresses specific advice in dealing with interactions with law enforcement .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Brooks et al. ( 2016 ) described the type of advice for those confronted by law enforcement while driving :

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Pulling over your vehicle right away Keeping hands visible on the steering wheel and not making sudden moves

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Not reaching for items in your wallet or glove compartment , without informing the law enforcement officer first Being as polite as possible , using " Yes sir , officer "

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Not arguing , even if you are right

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: The perception of a need for these behaviors has been described as racialized legal cynicism .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: According to PBS , the talks usually include instructions such as :

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: If you are stopped by the police : Always answer ' yes sir , no sir ' ; never talk back ; do n’t make any sudden movements ; do n’t put your hands in your pockets ; obey all commands ; if you think you are falsely accused , save it for the police station .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: I would rather pick you up at the station than the morgue … "

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: According to Vox , for Black people in the United States , " a typical police stop turning into a violent encounter is a very real , terrifying possibility . "

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Some Black parents focus on not only safety but also dignity and pride .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: There are five common general approaches parents take :

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Focusing primarily on pride in one ’s culture Discussing societal issues of injustice and inequality Focusing on the value of hard work and deemphasizing the importance of race Teaching messages of mistrust Avoidance of the discussion Parents often combine multiple approaches .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Research indicates the avoidance of discussion and teaching messages of mistrust are the least effective .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: Focusing on pride and societal issues is typically more effective .

source.page_title: The talk (racism in the United States)

text: The New York Times made a short documentary in 2015 featuring the experiences of Black Americans in having this conversation with their children and their memories of their own parents ' conversations with them .

text: " ... the terrorists have won " or " ... then the terrorists win " are rhetorical phrases which were widely used in the United States in the wake of the September 11 attacks .

source.page_title: The terrorists have won

text: In 1995 , an editorial about the response to the Oklahoma City bombing in the Ocala Star - Banner , of Ocala , Florida concluded : " Our response to terrorism should be carefully measured .

source.page_title: The terrorists have won

source.page_title: The terrorists have won

text: At the same time , an editorial in the Victoria Advocate of Victoria , Texas said : " If Americans begin to yield their own freedoms at home , the terrorists have won . "

source.page_title: The terrorists have won

source.page_title: The terrorists have won

text: The topos of ineffability ( German : Unsagbarkeitstopos ) is a rhetorical and philosophical motif referring to claims about the inadequacy of language to fully express certain experiences , objects , or forms of knowledge .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: The concept is used as a retrospective analytical category in the study of rhetoric , literature , theology , and philosophy , rather than as a self - designation employed by historical authors .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: The motif has been discussed in Western rhetorical and philosophical traditions from antiquity to modern theory , particularly in relation to metaphysical , aesthetic , and religious discourse .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: The term Unsagbarkeitstopos was systematized and popularized by the literary scholar Ernst Robert Curtius in his analysis of classical rhetorical topoi .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In this context , it denotes a conventional argumentative or stylistic pattern in which an author emphasizes that a subject exceeds the expressive capacities of language due to its magnitude , complexity , or transcendence .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In philosophical discourse , the topos of ineffability serves to articulate perceived limits of linguistic representation , particularly in discussions of metaphysical , aesthetic , or religious phenomena .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Historical background

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Antiquity Reflections on the limits of linguistic expression can already be found in classical Greek philosophy .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Plato repeatedly emphasizes the difficulty of adequately expressing ultimate principles , particularly in discussions of the Good and of non-being .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Such passages have often been interpreted by later commentators as anticipating themes of ineffability , although Plato himself does not formulate a systematic doctrine of the unsayable .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In Neoplatonism , the limits of discursive language become a central philosophical concern .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Plotinus argues that the One , as the highest principle of reality , transcends all predication and conceptual determination .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: He employs apophatic strategies , paradox , and appeals to silence in order to gesture toward what can not be expressed verbally .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Medieval theology and mysticism

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In medieval Christian thought , particularly in apophatic theology , the topos of ineffability becomes a prominent argumentative and theological motif .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Authors such as Pseudo - Dionysius the Areopagite emphasize divine transcendence through negation and paradox , highlighting the inadequacy of human language in relation to God .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Rhetoric and literature

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In rhetoric and literary theory , the topos of ineffability functions as a conventional device used to intensify emotional , aesthetic , or ethical impact .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: It appears , for example , in passages where authors claim that a subject can not be described adequately , thereby indirectly enhancing its perceived significance .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: The motif became especially prominent in early modern and Baroque literature , where themes of silence , excess , and inexpressibility were employed to signal transcendence or emotional intensity .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: During the Romantic period , reflections on the limits of language influenced aesthetic theory , particularly in German Romanticism .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In this context , the idea of “ absolute music ” emerged as an attempt to conceptualize artistic expression that operates beyond the constraints of propositional language .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Modern philosophy

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In modern philosophy , ineffability becomes a recurring topic in discussions of language , meaning , and experience .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Immanuel Kant associates the limits of conceptual language with aesthetic ideas , which stimulate thought without being fully determinable by concepts .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Such ideas , while not strictly unsayable , exceed the capacity of determinate conceptual articulation .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Ludwig Wittgenstein famously distinguishes between what can be said and what can only be shown , concluding the Tractatus Logico - Philosophicus with the proposition that “ whereof one can not speak , thereof one must be silent . ”

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: Contemporary discussions

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: In contemporary scholarship , the topos of ineffability is discussed across philosophy , linguistics , literary studies , and discourse analysis , particularly in relation to mystical experience , trauma , and other phenomena that challenge established modes of representation .

source.page_title: The topos of ineffability

text: See also Ineffability Apophatic theology Philosophy of language Rhetoric

text: Ernest Botherby , born in Perth in 1869 and died in Adelaide in 1944 , was " the scholar who founded the Australian school of ethnolinguistics , " for whom " the tribes of New Guinea " were " a favorite subject , " and who " rose to fame in the late 1920s after publishing several articles " on Pagolak .

text: Ohos and Ouhas

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Botherby 's first exploration , reported in The Case of the Persevering Maltese , takes place in the area of the central highlands of New Guinea , near the source of the Fly River .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Mathews provides details inspired by travel accounts from the late 19th century , such as that of Samuel Macfarlane :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Leaving from Tagota at the mouth of the Fly [ River ] , Botherby traveled upriver for more than 500 miles [ ... ] to finally reach the unexplored region he sought , a set of valleys located — using the toponymy of the time — between the Kaiserin Augusta , the Victor Emmanuel ranges , and the extension of the Musgrave range .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: It is the most linguistically complex region of New Guinea ( itself considered the most diverse region in the world in this respect , as nearly 1,000 languages are recorded there , often showing " enormous variation and many unusual features " ) , where even today , about a hundred Papuan languages , highly heterogeneous , are spoken .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: In a mountainous valley , Botherby discovers an archaic tribe of " a few hundred individuals , leading a peaceful existence under conditions of extreme simplicity . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: He names them the Ohos .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Their language is reduced to three words and a single expression : " Red equals bad , " although they make up for the poverty of their vocabulary by communicating through gestures , notably to indicate directions to Botherby or to express disagreement .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Continuing his exploration , Botherby discovers a second archaic tribe , which he names the Ouhas , whose language , just as rudimentary as that of the Ohos , only allows them to make " invariably the same statement " :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: " Here not there . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: A few weeks later , back in the Ohos valley and wishing to share his experience with them , he understands " what every translator learns sooner or later : a language says what it can say , and that 's all . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Thus , he has no choice but to translate " Here not there " as " Red equals bad . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This extreme experience allows Mathews to " playfully contradict " Jakobson 's assertion that " languages differ essentially in what they must convey and not in what they may convey . "

text: Le Dialecte de la tribu ( French translation ) , although published earlier , deals with events occurring after the discovery of the Ohos and the Ouhas .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This time , it concerns another tribe of New Guinea , speaking a language called " pagolak . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The short story takes the form of a letter in which the author reports his discovery of this language after reading a scientific article attributed to Dr. Botherby and titled Kalo gap pagolak , a title meaning " magical transformation of the pagolak . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Botherby 's article discusses the method used by the tribe speaking pagolak to translate expressions from their language into that of their neighbors — a method that produces translations that are " effective , " " intelligible and acceptable , " while hiding " the content , " the " primary meaning " of the original statements .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The kalo gap pagolak is more precisely the transcription of an oral statement by the abanika , the " chief of the word - chiefs " or " Chief of the Chief - Words " of the tribe , although the faculty of translation is not reserved for him : all members of the tribe who speak pagolak are capable of it .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Although pagolak is a " very primitive , " " rudimentary " language , and although there are two dictionaries ( one English , the other Dutch ) , these dictionaries , intended for traders , are arbitrary : they take into account only mercantile criteria and are of no use for understanding the translation method addressed in the kalo gap pagolak .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Botherby himself , although providing " useful " and even " very valuable " notes , has " no other choice but to leave the abanika 's statement intact " and provide no translation for it — a solution the narrator eventually applies to his letter .

text: The abanika 's statement is not made up of " words about a [ translation ] process " whose " substantial content " would need to be explained , but rather of " the words of the process in action ; " it is not " a description of the method , but the method itself . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: As a result , the narrator , following Dr. Botherby , claims he is capable of understanding the kalo gap without being able to reproduce it in another language .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French
