text: Questions of translation

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The issue of translation is central to the texts featuring Dr. Botherby , beginning with The Dialect of the Tribe .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: From the very first paragraph , the narrator evokes " the question of translation in general , " and in particular that of Perec 's works .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: He asserts : " Translation is the model , the archetype of all writing . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Furthermore , the second version includes an addition compared to the first , which Mariacarmela Mancarella considers " particularly significant : "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: How to translate a process ?

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: One would have to convey not only the words but also the silences between them ... as if trying to photograph the invisible air under a wing 's beat in mid-flight .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Impossible .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Mancarella sees in this a reference to the last sentence of Walter Benjamin 's The Task of the Translator :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: In some degree , all great writings , and most profoundly the sacred writings , contain their virtual translation between the lines .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The intralinear version of the sacred text is the archetype or ideal of all translation .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This fundamental issue is addressed from another angle in the first version of the story :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: You and I are well placed to know how false this [ notion of communication of a substantial content ] is and how translation , precisely , is an example of ' non - communication , ' an act that , in fact , dispels the illusion of substantial content .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: These statements suggest that the issue in the text is interlingual translation , the translation from one language to another .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Emily Apter considers that the story points to one of the " truisms of translation , " namely that something is always lost in translation and that , unless one " knows the language of the original , the exact nature of the loss will always be impossible to establish , and even if one has access to it , there is always an incompressible remainder of untranslatability that makes every translation an impossible world , a false regime of semantic and phonetic equivalence . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Furthermore , as Alison James emphasizes , in the case of translating Ouha into Oho , it is interlingual translation from one language to another that is at stake , with Mathews seeming concerned with " the inevitable transformation of meaning in the passage from one language or culture to another . "

text: Relationship to Quine and Wittgenstein

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Several authors believe that Dr. Botherby 's experiences evoke or illustrate Quine 's analyses on the indeterminacy of translation .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Quine , in Word and Object , asks the question : " How can the linguist know that his translation is correct ? "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: However , Mathews would substitute this question with : " What happens if the linguist knows that his translation will always be wrong ? "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Quine develops his analysis on this issue through what he calls the thought experiment of radical translation , illustrated by the example of the word gavagaï spoken by a native in the jungle at the emergence of a rabbit .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The linguist , attempting to understand what this word means , ends up associating it with the observational statement " look , a rabbit , " which can be confirmed by the assent of his interlocutor , yet the term does not lose its inscrutability .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Quine observes , it is unclear whether " the objects to which the term applies are not , after all , something like rabbits , for example , simple phases , brief temporal segments of rabbits ... or perhaps the objects to which ' gavagaï ' applies are only the parts , the still undivided pieces of these rabbits . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Quine notes that two independent dictionaries of this native language could present different and interchangeable content , each proposing a translation that the other would reject , while still describing the same behavior , which resembles the difficulties encountered in using the two dictionaries of pagolak .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Furthermore , Dr. Botherby 's disillusioned statement about the difficulty of translating the Ouhas ' claim , " Here , not there , " into the language of the Ohos , which can say " Red equals bad , " seems to echo Quine 's remark : " Who would attempt to translate ' neutrinos lack mass ' into a jungle language ? "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Mark Ford and Dennis Duncan , for their part , suggest that both the attempts at translating pagolak and the ouha in Mathews ' works and Perec 's notations about the Kubus resonate with Wittgenstein 's reflections on language games .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Perec reports an incidental remark by Appenzzell about the poverty of the Kubu vocabulary , exemplified by the polysemy of the term sinuya : " These characteristics could apply to a Western carpenter , who , using instruments with very precise names ... would ask his apprentice : ' Pass me the thing . ' "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This allusion , which the context of the novel does not require , refers , for Ford and Duncan , to a passage from Philosophical Investigations where Wittgenstein proposes a model of the " entire language of a tribe , " aiming to " dispel the fog by studying the language phenomena in the primitive forms of their usage that allow for a synoptic view of the purpose and function of words . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This " complete primitive language " consists of four words used in exchanges between a mason and his apprentice : " block , " " column , " " slab , " and " beam , " with the carpenter 's injunction in Perec echoing the mason 's command in Wittgenstein : " Slab ! " for " bring me the slab ! "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: For Duncan , it is " immediately apparent " that the example of the Ohos and Ouhas is intended to perform a " dispelling of the fog , " a modeling of the type Wittgenstein sought to carry out .

text: Relationship to Malinowski

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Marcel Appenzzell , the character in Life : A User 's Manual to whom Mathews ' Dr. Botherby refers , is presented by Perec as a student of Bronisław Malinowski , with whom he maintains correspondence and through whom he is introduced to Marcel Mauss , " who entrusted him at the Institute of Ethnology with the responsibility for a seminar on the ways of life of the Anadalams . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: In contrast , the short stories by Mathews where Dr. Botherby appears do not explicitly refer to Malinowski , but the connection is suggested by several clues : the period of scientific activity ( the 1920s ) , the field ( New Guinea ) , and the translation issues that Mathews places at the center of the texts where Botherby appears .

text: Moreover , both Quine 's and Wittgenstein 's analyses of language , which lead the former to employ the model of gavagaï and the latter to that of the mason , are inspired by or linked to Malinowski 's analyses .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Quine explicitly refers to these in Word and Object , and Ernest Gellner emphasizes the proximity of Wittgenstein 's analyses in Philosophical Investigations to the earlier thesis by Malinowski , which Wittgenstein may have encountered through Charles Kay Ogden , his English translator .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Malinowski provides a general formulation of his analysis in Le problème de la signification dans les langues primitives ( The Problem of Meaning in Primitive Languages ) , a text published in 1923 as an appendix to the book The Meaning of Meaning by Ogden and Ivor Armstrong Richards , in terms that resonate with Dr. Botherby 's considerations on the uselessness of dictionaries for understanding pagolak .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: He asserts that the available vocabularies of Oceanic languages , which at his time were primarily written by missionaries with the intent of helping their successors , limit themselves to providing the best possible approximation of a local term , without aiming , as a scientific translation would , to determine whether a word corresponds to an idea in the reader 's language or whether it corresponds to a completely foreign concept .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This is the case with beliefs , customs , ceremonies , or magical rites , for which it would be necessary to provide an " imaginary equivalent " and clarify its meaning through an ethnographic explanation .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Malinowski further asserts that in these languages , the use of metaphors , abstractions , and generalizations , combined with the concrete nature of expression , makes any simple and direct translation of words taken in isolation almost impossible , which leads him to develop the notion of " phatic communion , " a situation where social ties are created through the exchange of words and , consequently , the role of language in social interaction , emphasizing the importance of the position of words and the context of their usage .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: These analyses are developed in Coral Gardens , where he claims that the words of one language are never translatable into another and that the difficulty of translation increases with cultural specificities : " sport for England , good food and love - making for France ; sentimentality and metaphysical depths for Germany ; music , pasta , and painting for Italy . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: He therefore concludes that " if we understand ' to translate ' as finding verbal equivalents between two languages , this task is impossible , and the Italian proverb Traduttore , traditore is true . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: However , a translation is possible and correct if understood as cultural contextualization , and more specifically , as making the meaning of a word understood as the " effective change " it brings to a situation .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: As Bertrand Gervais points out , these aspects of phatic communication and performative value are precisely those that take precedence over the denotative function in both the Ohos and Ouhas , as well as in pagolak .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: A section of Coral Gardens is dedicated to a problem similar to the one Botherby encounters with pagolak : the translation of magical formulas .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Malinowski opts to render them in a " rhythmic and elaborate English version of the indigenous text , " believing that " in the original version , the magical language , with its wealth of phonetic , rhythmic , metaphoric , and alliterative effects , with its strange cadences and repetitions , has a prosodic character that must be conveyed to the reader , " without , however , taking too many liberties with it .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: He summarizes the difficulty as the translation of words that lack meaning , or more precisely , words whose function is not linked to their meaning but to a " magical influence that these words are supposed to exert . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Emphasizing that , in line with his theory of " phatic communion , " the meaning of any utterance is " the effective change it is supposed to bring about in the context of the situation in which it is uttered , " Malinowski highlights two aspects that guided his approach : the " coefficient of strangeness , " which he also calls the " element of nonsense , " meaning that some words are intended not to be understood , and are therefore intrinsically untranslatable ; and the " coefficient of intelligibility , " meaning that some words belong to everyday language and are intended to be understood .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The strangeness largely consists in an artificial form , in the non-standard use of certain roots , in repetitions or pairings [ ... ]

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The coefficient of intelligibility resides in the fact that the strangest formulations refer directly or indirectly to the subject on which the magic is focused .

text: In Life : A User 's Manual , the reference to Malinowski primarily serves to give a sense of reality to Appenzzell 's desire for exoticism , embedding it within the context of the participatory observation method Malinowski develops in The Argonauts of the Western Pacific , even though Perec 's ethnological reference may rather be the Lévi-Strauss of Tristes Tropiques .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: More generally , Perec shows a particular interest in applying an anthropological approach to daily life in his writing practice :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Perhaps it is about finally founding our anthropology : one that will speak of us , that will look within us for what we have long plundered from others .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Not the exotic , but the endotic .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: However , as Isabelle Dangy observes , this privileging of the endotic does not exclude , in a fictional context , the use of a " fictive , utopian , and semi- parodic ethnology " such as that developed in W or the Memory of Childhood , completed in 1975 just before Perec went to Montreal to collaborate on the commentary of Ahô : The Forest People .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Furthermore , as he claims in a 1976 interview , Perec believes that scientific knowledge plays a limited role in the development of his fictions , where it intervenes " not as truth , but as material , or machinery , of the imaginary . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: From an ethnolinguistic perspective , Appenzzell 's considerations are particularly close to the situation described by Botherby with the Ohos and the Ouhas : the Kubus , notes Perec 's ethnologist , use " an extremely reduced vocabulary , not exceeding a few dozen words , " a fact that leads Appenzzell to wonder whether , " like their distant neighbors , the Papuans , " the Kubus do not " deliberately impoverish their vocabulary , eliminating words each time there is a death in the village .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: One consequence of this fact is that a single word designates an increasingly larger number of objects . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This observation is a reference to A Void , where Perec quotes on the last page , among other quotes termed " metagraphs , " a 1937 geography manual by Étienne Baron :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Among the Papuans , the language is very poor ; each tribe has its language , and its vocabulary is constantly impoverishing because , after each death , some words are eliminated as a sign of mourning .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Perec probably read this quote from Barthes , who presents it in 1966 in Critique and Truth while commenting :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: On this point , we can teach the Papuans a lesson : we respectfully embalm the language of deceased writers and refuse the words , the new meanings that come into the world of ideas : the sign of mourning strikes here the birth , not the death .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This trope about Papuan language , often repeated elsewhere , contradicts a consistent note by Papuan language specialists .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: One of the first , Reverend Samuel Macfarlane , countered the then - popular opinion that the Papuans did not have a proper language , pointing out that , on the contrary , their languages are " in some respects superior to ours , " including in terms of vocabulary , some of which had words " as precise in their meaning as if they had been defined by Johnson . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: With this stereotype , Appenzzell diverges from the recommendations of his mentor , Malinowski , who , based on his fieldwork with the Trobrianders , argued that " the multiplicity of uses of each word is not due to any negative phenomenon such as mental confusion , poverty of language , perverse or careless usage . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Malinowski believes that the same word , used in a variety of meanings , " fulfills a very specific function , " that is , " to introduce a familiar element into an indefinite situation . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: To characterize this fact , Malinowski does not use the notion of polysemy or metaphor , but rather the concept of homonymy , asserting that it would be " erroneous to agglutinate all the meanings into a confused category " and condemning the " armchair anthropologist " who assumes a " pre-logical mentality " without " investigating the different meanings [ of a word ] or examining whether they are not true homonyms , that is , different words with the same sound . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This position , however , has been criticized : Edmund Leach describes the " doctrine of homonyms " as a " desperate expedient , " and Quine observes that Malinowski , wishing to " spare " the Trobrianders from an accusation of prelogical thinking , multiplies the translations of the same word according to the context to avoid any contradiction .

text: Interlingual or intralingual translation ?

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: If this example is ambivalent , as it contains both an interlingual dimension ( the translation of Kafka into French ) and an intralingual dimension ( the rewriting of it ) , the intralingual conception of translation , within the same language , emerges in the article Translation from the Oulipo Compendium , where Harry Mathews states that translation is " a central principle of Oulipian research , but not in the usual sense of the term ; Oulipian translation techniques are used within the same language , and each technique manipulates an element of the text that has been artificially isolated from the whole , whether it concerns meaning , sound , grammar , or vocabulary . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Mathews summarizes his point of view for journalist Lynne Tillman : " Perhaps writing is nothing but a translation — in the end , a translation that does n't want to be identified as such , " an assertion that carries two aspects : on the one hand , the position of writing as transformation , as manipulation through constraints , an analysis shared within the Oulipo ; and on the other hand , Mathews ' personal choice not to reveal the constraints he uses , thus giving the impression of " following rules from elsewhere , " much like Raymond Queneau and in contrast to Perec ( who , however , does not reveal all of them ) .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: In this sense , according to Bertrand Gervais , Le Dialecte de la tribu " seems to speak , with its practice of the kalo gap pagolak , about interlingual translation , when it only speaks of intralingual translation , which is at the heart of Oulipian practice . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: In this sense , the narrator 's statement can be interpreted in the story : " One could say that , insofar as true writing is a form of translation , the text from which it operates is infinitely difficult since it is nothing less than the universe itself . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: For Gervais , Mathews ' story is a trompe - l'œil :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: [ It ] manages to confuse critics and theorists who fall for the illusion of the represented object .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Perhaps , due to an expectation horizon exclusively focused on translation and its theories , the artifice proves particularly powerful , and the screen is mistaken for the thing itself .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: The tribute , with its allusive system , taking the form of a text with ethnological character and a narrative style like Raymond Roussel , has become a realistic text , and the translation has transformed from a metaphor of writing under constraint into a true interlingual translation .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: To highlight this dimension of intralingual translation at work in the pagolak , Thomas Beebee emphasizes one aspect : the use of the palindrome .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: He observes that the very name of the magical method , kalo gap , is a palindrome of pagolak ; that the two components of the method , namalam ( the end ) and namele ( the means ) , are quasi -palindromes ; that nanmana ( the initiatory rite ) is an analogical transformation of namalan ; that as the text progresses toward its conclusion , the palindromes become more " monstrous , " such as nasavuloniputitupinoluvasan , a large palindrome that contains a small one , tit , in its center ; that the final exhortation , which the narrator no longer bothers to translate , is also palindromic ; that it again has tit at its center and uses , in at least one sense , all the words of pagolak previously employed :

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Amak kalo gap eleman nama la n'kat tokkele sunawa setan amnan wnanisi sutu pakotisovulisanan unafat up lenumo kona kafe avanu lo se akina ba nasavuloniputitupinoluvasan ( !! ) abanika esolunava efaka nok omunel put afanu nansiluvo sitokap utu sis namu nanmana tes awa nuselek kot tak nalaman namele Pagolak kama .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: According to Bertrand Gervais , the Oulipian dimension of the intralingual game takes precedence , in Le Dialecte de la tribu , over the apparent discourse regarding interlingual translation : it is not only a tribute to one of the most prominent members of Oulipo , Georges Perec , but also a " self - reflexive " text about Oulipo as a " literary and interpretative community , " as a tribe , and about its dialect .

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: Moreover , as Camille Bloomfield and Hermes Salceda observe , both dimensions of translation , interlingual and intralingual , combine in Oulipian text translation , aiming to " produce in the target language an effect comparable to that produced by the source text in the source culture . "

source.page_title: The translation of The Dialect of the Tribe in French

text: This is , for example , the ambition of Umberto Eco 's Italian translation of Raymond Queneau 's Exercises in Style , about which the translator states : " One must , rather than translate , recreate in another language . "

text: In Buddhism , acinteyya ( Pali ) , " imponderable " or " incomprehensible , " avyākṛta ( Sanskrit : अव्याकृत , Pali : avyākata , " unfathomable , unexpounded , " ) , and atakkāvacara , " beyond the sphere of reason , " are unanswerable questions or undeclared questions .

source.page_title: The unanswerable questions

text: They are sets of questions that should not be thought about , and which the Buddha refused to answer , since this distracts from practice , and hinders the attainment of liberation .

source.page_title: The unanswerable questions

text: " The war to end war " ( now commonly phrased " the war to end all wars " ; originally from the 1914 book The War That Will End War by H. G. Wells ) is a term for the First World War ( 1914 – 1918 ) .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: Originally an idealistic slogan , it is now mainly used sardonically , since not only was the First World War not history 's final war , but its aftermath also indirectly contributed to the outbreak of the even more devastating Second World War ( 1939 – 1945 ) .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: Origin During August 1914 , immediately after the outbreak of the war , English author and social commentator H. G. Wells published a number of articles in London newspapers that subsequently appeared as a book entitled The War That Will End War .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: He blamed the Central Powers for starting the war and argued that only the defeat of German militarism could bring about an end .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: He used the shorter form , " the war to end war " , for In the Fourth Year ( 1918 ) , in which he noted that the phrase " got into circulation " in the second half of 1914 .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: It became one of the most common catchphrases of the First World War .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: Later use During the First World War , the phrase met with some degree of skepticism .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: As it became apparent that the war had not succeeded in ending war , the phrase took on a more cynical tone .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: The British staff officer Archibald Wavell , a future field marshal and viceroy of India , said despondently of the Paris Peace Conference : " After the ' war to end war ' , they seem to have been pretty successful in Paris at making the ' Peace to end Peace ' . "

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: Wells himself used the phrase in an ironic way in the novel The Bulpington of Blup ( 1932 ) .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: Walter Lippmann in 1967 noted : " The delusion is that whatever war we are fighting is the war to end war " , while U.S. President Richard Nixon in his " Silent Majority " speech ( 1969 ) said : " I do not tell you that the war in Vietnam is the war to end wars " .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: Since at least the last third of the 20th century , the alternative wording " the war to end all wars " has increasingly become popular .

source.page_title: The war to end war

text: " The War to End All Wars " has been used by authors such as Edward M. Coffman ( 1968 ) , Russell Freedman ( 2010 ) and Adam Hochschild ( 2011 ) .

text: The wave or the new wave of post - hardcore ( TNWOPH ) was a loosely - defined collective of post - hardcore bands and the movement that spawned around them .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Taking place between roughly 2008 and 2015 , it was founded by Defeater , La Dispute , Make Do and Mend , Pianos Become the Teeth and Touché Amoré .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The movement was a reaction against the commerciality of the pop screamo sound , which had dominated the post - hardcore scene for much of the 2000s .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: In response , bands in the wave embraced the influence of screamo , melodic hardcore and post - rock , as well as literary forms , often spoken word .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: By 2012 , the wave had come to encompass a spectrum of bands that were similar to , influenced by or friends with the founding acts of the movement .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: This included contemporary screamo bands State Faults , the Saddest Landscape , Frameworks and Caravels , bands also in the emo revival such as Balance and Composure , Title Fight and Tigers Jaw , blackgaze band Deafheaven , and Britain 's UKswell movement , which included the Goodtime Boys and Bastions .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The wave declined in 2015 , when Touché Amoré , La Dispute and Pianos Become the Teeth entered hiatuses .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: By this point , it s influence had repopularized melodic hardcore , pushed many bands to embrace the influence of post - rock and pioneered the dreamcore genre .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The term " The Wave " was initially coined as an inside joke .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: This self - descriptor encompassed only Touché Amoré , La Dispute , Defeater , Pianos Become the Teeth and Make Do and Mend , who believed that collectively , they were similar to the group of bands that made up Revolution Summer .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Brad Vander Lugt of La Dispute commented on how the term has been interpreted with more serious attitude from people , saying : " people just ran with it and some kids took it really seriously , like we were trying to create some kind of collective , which it was n't at all .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: But we are really good friends with all of those bands .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: They 're like brothers to us and I think , in that way , it is a collective . "

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Overland called it a " tree house club " .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The movement ran parallel to the emo revival , and as , around 2013 , the definition of " emo revival " expanded , some of the major groups in the wave began to also be considered a part of the emo revival .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Bands in the wave were largely reviving 1990s emo , screamo and post - hardcore sounds , with some instead playing pop-punk and punk rock .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The Guardian described the wave as having heavy lyrical emphasis , in a way reminiscent of 1990s emo When used as a genre label , the wave encompasses an " overwrought " style of emo that combines elements of melodic hardcore , screamo and post -rock .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: It makes use of screamed vocals and ambient soundscapes within the context of 1990s - style screamo .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Many bands disregarded the conventional boundaries of hardcore at the time , instead embracing outside influences and touring with groups of different genres .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Stereogum writer Ellie Kovach described it as " the sonic cross-section of uncompromisingly independent and abrasive ' 90s hardcore and the kind of warmly melodic sensibilities and accessible vulnerability that had turned emo into an explosive juggernaut at the turn of the century . "

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Veil of Sound noted it as having an " affinity with adding many little twists and elements in order to maintain a certain unpredictability " .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Treblezine writer Tom Morgan called the term " nebulous " because " The bands it encompassed were just too disparate " , noting their major similarities as being their experimentalism , their use of melodrama and their difficulty to categorize into established music genres .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: Origins During the 2000s , post - hardcore had developed from an experimental DIY hardcore punk genre into what Stereogum writer Ellie Kovach called " a meaningless term ... codified and commodified into something sleek and polished , the likes of which hardcore had initially willed itself into existence to spite . "

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The wave was a rejection of these developments , which Jeremy Bolm of Touché Amoré described as " years of awful , awful , awful insincere garbage that has taken over everything for so long now and I 'd like to hope that it 's starting to get weeded out … you know , like , the terrible swoop hair , rock star attitude , bullshit breakdown bands that have nothing to really offer anybody " .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The wave grew out of the more literary side of 2000s melodic hardcore , where Last Lights and the Carrier were writing concept albums .

source.page_title: The wave (music)

text: The welcome arrival of rain is an orchestral composition written between 2001 and 2002 by the British composer Judith Weir .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: It was commissioned for the centennial celebration of the Minnesota Orchestra , which first performed the piece under the conductor Osmo Vänskä on 22 January 2003 .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: The welcome arrival of rain is written in a single movement and lasts about 16 minutes .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: The work 's title was inspired by a passage from the Hindu text Bhagavata Purana and the music itself was inspired in part by the annual arrival of the monsoon in India .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: The work is scored for a large orchestra comprising three flutes ( 3rd doubling piccolo ) , two oboes , cor anglais , three clarinets , three bassoons , four horns , four trumpets , timpani , three percussionists ( on glockenspiel , rototoms , and tomtoms ) , harp , and strings .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: Reception Reviewing the United Kingdom premiere by the BBC Symphony Orchestra , Andrew Clements of The Guardian called The welcome arrival of rain " an enchanting piece " and wrote , " the elements of Weir 's quarter - hour orchestral evocation seem simple enough — a recurrent Janacek - like brass refrain , a pattering of drums that sets in halfway through and gets more insistent , a pawky trio of bassoons , sky - bound flutes , flaring clarinets — but these ingredients are combined in unexpected ways , through sly orchestral doublings and sleights of pacing . "

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: Tom Service , also writing for The Guaridan , later named the piece as one of five key works in the composer 's career .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: Geoffrey Norris of The Daily Telegraph was slightly more critical of the work , however , observing , " The ending to this piece , in part inspired by a Hindu text about the monsoon , has a sweet freshness to it , but the rest is harder to fathom .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: As one who normally responds keenly to Weir 's music and likes its healthy diversity , I found The Welcome Arrival of Rain slightly disappointing .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: The mounting energy of which Weir spoke in her programme note did not really materialise . "

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: He added , " The music is certainly written with a virtuoso flourish , with plenty of instrumental colour and atmosphere .

source.page_title: The welcome arrival of rain

text: A firm rhythmic momentum is maintained , but the texture becomes mired in detail and a profusion of material , and somehow loses a sense of structural grip and direction . "

text: " the wizard " is the sixth episode of the fourth season of the American crime tragicomedy television series Barry .

text: The series follows Barry Berkman , a hitman from Cleveland who travels to Los Angeles to kill someone but finds himself joining an acting class taught by Gene Cousineau , where he meets aspiring actress Sally Reed and begins to question his path in life as he deals with his criminal associates such as Monroe Fuches and NoHo Hank .

text: A theatre director or stage director is a professional in the theatre field who oversees and orchestrates the mounting of a theatre production such as a play , opera , dance , drama , musical theatre performance , etc. by unifying various endeavors and aspects of production .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The director 's function is to ensure the quality and completeness of the theatre production and to lead the members of the creative team into realizing their artistic vision for it .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The director thereby collaborates with a team of creative individuals and other staff to coordinate research and work on all the aspects of the production which includes the Technical and the Performance aspects .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The technical aspects include : stagecraft , costume design , theatrical properties ( props ) , lighting design , set design , and sound design for the production .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The performance aspects include : acting , dance , orchestra , chants , and stage combat .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: If the production is a new piece of writing or a ( new ) translation of a play , the director may also work with the playwright or a translator .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: In contemporary theatre , after the playwright , the director is generally the principle visionary , making decisions on the artistic conception and interpretation of the play and its staging .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Different directors occupy different places of authority and responsibility , depending on the structure and philosophy of individual theatre companies .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Directors use a wide variety of techniques , philosophies , and levels of collaboration .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The director in theatre history

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: In ancient Greece , the birthplace of European drama , the writer bore principal responsibility for the staging of his plays .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Actors were generally semi-professionals , and the director oversaw the mounting of plays from the writing process all the way through to their performance , often acting in them too , as Aeschylus for example did .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The author - director would also train the chorus , sometimes compose the music , and supervise every aspect of production .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The fact that the director was called didaskalos , the Greek word for " teacher , " indicates that the work of these early directors combined instructing their performers with staging their work .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: In medieval times , the complexity of vernacular religious drama , with its large scale mystery plays that often included crowd scenes , processions and elaborate effects , gave the role of director ( or stage manager or pageant master ) considerable importance .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: A miniature by Jean Fouquet from 1460 ( pictured ) bears one of the earliest depictions of a director at work .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Holding a prompt book , the central figure directs , with the aid of a long stick , the proceedings of the staging of a dramatization of the Martyrdom of Saint Apollonia .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: According to Fouquet , the director 's tasks included overseeing the erecting of a stage and scenery ( there were no permanent , purpose - built theatre structures at this time , and performances of vernacular drama mostly took place in the open air ) , casting and directing the actors ( which included fining them for those that infringed rules ) , and addressing the audience at the beginning of each performance and after each intermission .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: From Renaissance times up until the 19th century , the role of director was often carried by the actor - manager .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: This would usually be a senior actor in a troupe who took the responsibility for choosing the repertoire of work , staging it and managing the company .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: This was the case for instance with Commedia dell'arte companies and English actor - managers like Colley Cibber and David Garrick .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The modern theatre director can be said to have originated in the staging of elaborate spectacles of the Meininger Company under George II , Duke of Saxe - Meiningen .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The management of large numbers of extras and complex stagecraft matters necessitated an individual to take on the role of overall coordinator .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: This gave rise to the role of the director in modern theatre , and Germany would provide a platform for a generation of emerging visionary theatre directors , such as Erwin Piscator and Max Reinhardt .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Simultaneously , Konstantin Stanislavski , principally an actor - manager , would set up the Moscow Art Theatre in Russia and similarly emancipate the role of the director as artistic visionary .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The French regisseur is also sometimes used to mean a stage director , most commonly in ballet .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: A more common term for theatre director in French is metteur en scène .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Post World War II , the actor - manager slowly started to disappear , and directing become a fully fledged artistic activity within the theatre profession .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: The director originating artistic vision and concept , and realizing the staging of a production , became the norm rather than the exception .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Great forces in the emancipation of theatre directing as a profession were notable 20th - century theatre directors like Vladimir Nemirovich - Danchenko , Vsevolod Meyerhold , Yevgeny Vakhtangov , Michael Chekhov , Yuri Lyubimov ( Russia ) , Orson Welles , Peter Brook , Peter Hall ( Britain ) , Bertolt Brecht ( Germany ) , Giorgio Strehler , and Franco Zeffirelli ( Italy ) .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: A cautionary note was introduced by the famed director Sir Tyrone Guthrie who said " the only way to learn how to direct a play , is ... to get a group of actors simple enough to allow you to let you direct them , and direct . "

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: A number of seminal works on directing and directors include Toby Cole and Helen Krich 's 1972 Directors on Directing : A Sourcebook of the Modern Theatre , Edward Braun 's 1982 book The Director and the Stage : From Naturalism to Growtowski , and Will 's The Director in a Changing Theatre ( 1976 ) .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Directing education Because of the relatively late emergence of theatre directing as a performing arts profession when compared with for instance acting or musicianship , a rise of professional vocational training programmes in directing can be seen mostly in the second half of the 20th century .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Most European countries nowadays know some form of professional directing training , usually at drama schools or conservatoires , or at universities .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: In Britain , the tradition that theatre directors emerge from degree courses ( usually in English literature ) at the Oxbridge universities has meant that for a long time , professional vocational training did not take place at drama schools or performing arts colleges , although an increase in training programmes for theatre directors can be witnessed since the 1970s and 1980s .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: In American universities , the seminal directing program at the Yale School of Drama produced a number of pioneering directors with D.F.A. ( Doctor of Fine Arts ) and M.F.A. degrees in Drama ( rather than English ) who contributed to the expansion of professional resident theaters in the 1960s and 1970s .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: In the early days such programmes typically led to the staging of one major thesis production in the third ( final ) year .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: At the University of California , Irvine , Keith Fowler ( a Yale D.F.A. and ex-producer of two LORT companies ) led for many years a graduate programme based on the premise that directors are autodidacts who need as many opportunities to direct as possible .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Under Fowler , graduate student directors would stage between five and ten productions during their three - year residencies , with each production receiving detailed critiques .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: As with many other professions in the performing arts , theatre directors would often learn their skills " on the job " ; to this purpose , theatres often employ trainee assistant directors or have in - house education schemes to train young theatre directors .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Examples are the Royal National Theatre in London , which frequently organizes short directing courses , or the Orange Tree Theatre and the Donmar Warehouse on London 's West End , which both employ resident assistant directors on a one - year basis for training purposes .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Styles of directing Directing is an art form that has grown with the development of theatre theory and theatre practice .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: With the emergence of new trends in theatre , so too have directors adopted new methodologies and engaged in new practices .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Interpretation of the drama , by the late twentieth century , had become central to the director 's work .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Relativism and psychoanalytic theory influenced the work of innovative directors such as Peter Brook , Ingmar Bergman , Peter Hall , Peter Stein , and Giorgio Strehler .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Kimberly Senior , director of Disgraced on Broadway , explains her role as director by saying “ I get to take things that were previously in one dimension and put them into three dimensions using my imagination and intellect and people skills . ”

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: Once a show has opened ( premiered before a regular audience ) , theatre directors are generally considered to have fulfilled their function .

source.page_title: Theatre director

text: From that point forward the stage manager is left in charge of all essential concerns .

text: Saint Thecla of Kitzingen ( Tecla of England , Heilga ) ( died ca. AD 790 ) was an Anglo - Saxon Benedictine nun , abbess , and missionary .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: She was among several figures associated with Saint Boniface and the Anglo - Saxon mission .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Background Sometime after the death of Aldfrith of Northumbria around the year 705 , his widow , Cuthburh , the sister of King Ine of Wessex , established a double - monastery in her brother 's kingdom at Wimborne in Dorset .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: St. Richard of Wessex was one of the underkings of the West Saxons and married Winna , the sister of St. Boniface .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Before starting on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land with his two sons , Richard entrusted his eleven - year - old daughter Walpurga to the abbess of Wimborne .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: The nuns of Wimborne Abbey educated Walpurga , and she later became a community member .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Boniface kept up a frequent correspondence with the community of Wimborne .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Life Born in southern Britain , Thecla was a relative of Saint Lioba .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Thecla and Lioba were educated at Wimborne Abbey and later joined the Benedictine community of nuns there .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: When Boniface wrote to the Abbess Tetta , requesting helpers with his missionary work in Germany , Thecla and Lioba were among those sent .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Boniface seems to have had a threefold purpose in summoning these Anglo - Saxon nuns as his auxiliaries : to propagate the full observance of the Benedictine Rule by new foundations , to introduce it into already founded monasteries , and to restore its observance in others , and finally , to bring their gentle influence to bear on the local people , both by example and by the education imparted to their children .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: In 748 , they arrived in Bischofsheim ( " bishop 's place " ) , where Boniface founded a convent , and Lioba was made abbess .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Later , Thecla became abbess of Ochsenfurt .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Sometime after 750 , upon the death of Hadelonga , foundress and first Abbess of Kitzingen on the Main , she was also called to supervise that abbey .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Her feast day is 15 October , but alternative feast days of 27 or 28 September also appear in liturgical books .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: Thecla ’s relics were enshrined during the Middle Ages at Kitzingen but were later dispersed during the German Peasants ' War .

source.page_title: Thecla of Kitzingen

text: She is also venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church .

text: The Theophile Bruguier Cabin is a historic building located in Sioux City , Iowa , United States .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: Bruguier was a Quebec native who was a trader with the American Fur Company .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: He was the first Caucasian settler in what would become Sioux City .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: He settled at the confluence of the Missouri and the Big Sioux Rivers in 1849 .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: With him were his two wives , Dawn and Blazing Cloud , and his father - in - law War Eagle , a chief of Yankton tribe , and extended family .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: He built a number of log structures on his 560 - acre ( 230 ha ) claim .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: Bruguier took up farming and set up his own fur - trading company .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: War Eagle and his two daughters , Bruguier 's wives , died in the 1850s .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: Bruguier sold a tract of land to Joseph Leonnais in 1855 , and it became the original townsite for Sioux City .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: He built this single - room cabin for his home about 1860 , and married Victoria Brunette in 1862 .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: Bruguier and his wife moved to a farm near Salix , Iowa , where he died in 1895 .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: In time , the cabin was covered with a wood veneer on the outside and plaster on the inside .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: It was discovered when the Rev. John Hantla of the Wall Street Mission was tearing it down .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: Workers from the Civil Works Administration dismantled the cabin and rebuilt it in Riverside Park in 1934 .

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: Two years later , it was dedicated as a memorial to the " friendly Indians of the Sioux nation who lived in peace with the early pioneers , " and to " Theophile Bruguier , the first permanent white resident within the present boundary of Sioux City . "

source.page_title: Theophile Bruguier Cabin

text: The cabin was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2000 .

text: This Is True is a syndicated weekly newspaper column and electronic mailing list written by American humorist and journalist Randy Cassingham .

source.page_title: This is True

text: The column describes strange - but - true stories culled from news sources around the globe , each ending with a humorous observation .

source.page_title: This is True

text: Cassingham reports that there are more than 44,000 subscribers to the mailing list for True .

source.page_title: This is True

text: Frequent themes in This is True include absurd governmental actions or policies , unusual or badly phrased newspaper headlines , and injuries and deaths due to outrageous negligence ( similar to the Darwin Awards ) .

source.page_title: This is True

text: Cassingham particularly favors stories of outrageous effects of zero tolerance policies in schools , such as children expelled ( under drugs rules ) for sharing cough drops .

source.page_title: This is True

text: Cassingham has been criticized for repeating myths and lies regarding many of the stories published in " This is True " .

text: This is the Coast is a local radio station serving the Yorkshire coastal areas of Scarborough , Filey , Whitby , Bridlington , and Hornsea .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: This is the Coast launched in October 2020 to provide a local radio service for the Yorkshire Coast after the area 's previous local station , Yorkshire Coast Radio , became part of a national radio network .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: Initially the station launched online and smart speakers before obtaining an Ofcom DAB licence later in the month .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: The station features locally focused content throughout all of its live programming hours , reacting to the events of the day .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: Local presenters include Paddy Billington , Tom Hooper , Mike Nicholson , Darren Lethem , Tom Ironside , Richard Simister and Chris Johnson .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: This is the Coast broadcasts hourly news bulletins , with headlines on the half - hour during weekday breakfast .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: The bulletins have a strong local focus with a team of in - house journalists also producing content for the station 's website and smartphone app .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: The news team consists of Matthew Pells , Shaun Moore and Andrew Snaith .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: National material is provided by Sky News Radio .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: This is the Coast can be heard on DAB + across North Yorkshire on the Muxco multiplex .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: The station extended its coverage in March 2024 by joining the MuxCo Lincolnshire & Humberside DAB multiplex .

source.page_title: This is the Coast

text: The station is also available online , on its own smartphone apps and on smart speakers .

text: Thomas , 2nd Earl of Lancaster ( c. 1278 – 22 March 1322 ) was an English nobleman of the first House of Lancaster , a cadet branch of the royal Plantagenet dynasty .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: He held the titles of Earl of Lancaster , Leicester , and Derby from 1296 until his death in 1322 , and also those of Earl of Lincoln and Salisbury jure uxoris from 1311 to 1322 .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: As one of the most powerful barons in England , Thomas became a leading figure in the baronial opposition to his first cousin , King Edward II .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Early life and marriage Thomas was the eldest son of Edmund Crouchback and Blanche of Artois , Queen Dowager of Navarre and niece of King Louis IX of France .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Crouchback was a son of King Henry III of England .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Through his mother , Thomas was a half - brother of Queen Joan I of Navarre .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: His marriage to Alice de Lacy was not successful .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: They had no children together , while he fathered , illegitimately , two sons named John and Thomas .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: In 1317 , Alice was abducted from her manor at Canford , Dorset , by Richard de St Martin , a knight in the service of John de Warenne , 7th Earl of Surrey .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: This incident caused a feud between Lancaster and Surrey ; Lancaster seized two of Surrey 's castles in retaliation .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: King Edward then intervened , and the two earls came to an uneasy truce .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Thomas continued to hold the powerful earldoms of Lincoln and Salisbury .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: This was due to the marriage contract the two families had agreed upon ; upon the death of his father - in - law , Thomas would hold these earldoms in his own right , not , as would be expected , in right of his wife .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Earl of Lancaster

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: On reaching full age , he became hereditary sheriff of Lancashire .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: However , he spent most of the next ten years fighting for Edward I in Scotland , leaving the shrievalty in the care of deputies .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: He was present at the Battle of Falkirk in 1298 as part of Edward I 's wing of the army .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: He served in the coronation of his cousin , King Edward II of England , on 25 February 1308 , carrying Curtana , the sword of Edward the Confessor .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: At the beginning of the king 's reign , Lancaster openly supported Edward , but as the conflict between the king and the nobles wore on , Lancaster 's allegiances changed .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: He despised the royal favourite , Piers Gaveston , who mocked him as " the Fiddler " and swore revenge when Gaveston demanded that the king dismiss one of Lancaster 's retainers .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Lancaster was one of the Lords Ordainers who demanded the banishment of Gaveston and the establishment of a baronial oligarchy .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: His private army helped separate the king and Gaveston , and Lancaster was one of the " judges " who convicted Gaveston and saw him executed in 1312 .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: After the disaster at Bannockburn in 1314 , Edward submitted to Lancaster , who in effect became ruler of England .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: He attempted to govern for the next four years , but could not keep order or prevent the Scots from raiding and retaking territory in the North .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: In 1318 , his popularity with the barons declined , and he was persuaded " to accept a diminished authority " .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: The new leadership , eventually headed by Hugh le Despenser , 1st Earl of Winchester , and his son Hugh Despenser the Younger , proved no more popular with the baronage , and in 1321 Lancaster was again at the head of a rebellion .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: This time , he was defeated at the Battle of Boroughbridge on 16 March 1322 and taken prisoner .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Lancaster was tried by a tribunal consisting of , among others , the two Despensers ; Edmund Fitzalan , 9th Earl of Arundel ; and King Edward .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Lancaster was not allowed to speak in his defence , nor was he allowed to have anyone speak for him .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: He was convicted of treason and sentenced to death .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Because of their kinship and Lancaster 's royal blood , the king commuted the sentence to beheading , as opposed to being hanged , drawn and beheaded , and Lancaster was executed on 22 March 1322 near Pontefract Castle .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Upon his death , his titles and estates were forfeited , and the Scots , whom Lancaster gained aid from in his rebellion , mainly to weaken the English in their war , seized the opportunity to take his inheritance in the Great Raid of 1322 .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: In 1323 , his younger brother Henry successfully petitioned to take possession of the earldom of Leicester , and in 1326 or 1327 , Parliament posthumously reversed Thomas 's conviction .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Henry was further permitted to take possession of the earldoms of Lancaster , Derby , Salisbury and Lincoln .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Soon after Thomas 's death , miracles were reported at his tomb at Pontefract , and he became venerated as a martyr and saint .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: In 1327 , the Commons petitioned Edward III to ask for his canonisation , and popular veneration continued until the reformation .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: In 1822 , it was alleged that Thomas 's remains had been discovered on Monday 25 March of that year , in a large stone coffin buried in a field in the parish of Ferry Fryston ( precisely five hundred years after his execution and precisely one week before April Fools ' Day ) .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: This story was syndicated in stereotype in the first week of April , credited to " the Leeds Mercury of Saturday last " ( i.e. 30 March 1822 ) ; in the second week of April syndicated in a new stereotype without crediting the Mercury ( and paired with an apparently true story about the February discovery in Capelle of a " fossil ship " ) ; and then disappeared from the public eye .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: In 1942 , E. J. Rudsdale wrote that he had encountered a box of bones , labeled as Thomas 's and as having been " removed from Pomfret Castle " in 1885 , at Paskell 's auctioneers in Colchester , Essex .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Titles and lands

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Thomas inherited the earldoms of Lancaster , Leicester and the Ferrers earldom of Derby from his father .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: By his marriage to Alice de Lacy , Countess of Lincoln , daughter and heiress of Henry de Lacy , 3rd Earl of Lincoln , he became Earl of Lincoln , Earl of Salisbury , 11th Baron of Halton and 7th Lord of Bowland upon the death of his father - in - law in 1311 .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Master of five earldoms , he was one of England 's wealthiest and most powerful men .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Thomas was in possession of many key fortresses , including Clitheroe Castle , particularly in northern England .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: He was responsible for the extension of Pontefract Castle , and in 1313 , he began the construction of Dunstanburgh Castle , a massive fortress in Northumberland .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Arms Inherited from his father , Thomas bore the arms of the kingdom , differenced by a label France of three points ( that is to say , azure three fleur - de - lys or , each ) .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: Genealogical table Thomas was closely related to the Capetian kings of France and the Plantagenet kings of England .

source.page_title: Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster

text: His contemporaries commented , " as each parent was of royal stock , he was clearly of nobler descent than the other earls " .
